subject: physics

items.q: A pure substance is heated steadily from a solid until it has completely boiled. According to the molecular model, which statement about its molecules is correct?
items.correct: Their mean separation changes little on melting but increases greatly on boiling.
items.misconception: Their mean separation increases greatly on melting and increases again on boiling.
items.why: Many simple diagrams draw liquid particles with visible gaps between them, and students assume the three states must be evenly spaced steps. Flow is wrongly explained by space between particles rather than by particles not being held in fixed positions. Densities show the truth: ice and water differ by about 10%, but water and steam at 100 °C differ by a factor of about 1600. A liquid flows because its particles, though close together, are not held in fixed positions and can slide past one another.
items.specStatementText: molecular theory in solids, liquids and gases
items.random_wrong: The molecules themselves get larger on melting, and larger again on boiling.

items.q: At 100 °C and atmospheric pressure, liquid water has a density of 958 kg m⁻³ and steam has a density of 0.598 kg m⁻³. What do these data show about the molecules in steam compared with those in the liquid water?
items.correct: Their mean separation is about 12 times larger, as the volume per molecule is 1600 times larger.
items.misconception: Their mean separation is about 1600 times larger, because the density is 1600 times smaller.
items.why:
Students learn 1 m = 100 cm and apply the same factor to squared and cubed units. Proportional reasoning about area and volume is a documented difficulty (Arons, 'Teaching Introductory Physics'), and it persists into university. Write the unit or length out in full and apply the power: (10⁻² m)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³; A = 4πr² so A ∝ r²; V ∝ separation³ so separation ∝ V^(1/3).

Working: Density ratio = 958/0.598 = 1602 ≈ 1600. For the same mass (same number of identical molecules), the volume per molecule is ≈ 1600 times larger in steam. Mean separation ∝ (volume per molecule)^(1/3), so the ratio of separations = 1602^(1/3) = 11.7 ≈ 12.
items.specStatementText: molecular theory in solids, liquids and gases
items.random_wrong: Each molecule is about 1600 times larger, so each one takes up 1600 times the space.
items.working: Density ratio = 958/0.598 = 1602 ≈ 1600. For the same mass (same number of identical molecules), the volume per molecule is ≈ 1600 times larger in steam. Mean separation ∝ (volume per molecule)^(1/3), so the ratio of separations = 1602^(1/3) = 11.7 ≈ 12.

items.q: The density of aluminium is 2.7 g cm⁻³. What is the volume, in m³, of an aluminium block of mass 0.081 kg?
items.why:
Many GCSE calculations use convenient units throughout, and students treat unit conversion as a formality rather than part of the physics. Convert first: g → kg (÷ 1000), cm → m (÷ 100), cm³ → m³ (÷ 10⁶), ly → m (× 9.46 × 10¹⁵). Then the constant's units (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, W m⁻² K⁻⁴) match and the answer comes out in SI.

Working: ρ = m/V ⇒ V = m/ρ. In SI: ρ = 2.7 g cm⁻³ = 2.7 × 10³ kg m⁻³; V = 0.081 kg/(2.7 × 10³ kg m⁻³) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³ (= 30 cm³).
items.specStatementText: density ρ as given by ρ = m/V
items.working: ρ = m/V ⇒ V = m/ρ. In SI: ρ = 2.7 g cm⁻³ = 2.7 × 10³ kg m⁻³; V = 0.081 kg/(2.7 × 10³ kg m⁻³) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³ (= 30 cm³).

items.q: Liquefied natural gas is stored at 112 K, the boiling point of methane at atmospheric pressure. What is this temperature on the Celsius scale?
items.why:
Students first meet the conversion as 'add 273' (°C to K), the direction used most often, and memorize the operation rather than the relationship T/K = θ/°C + 273. Use the relationship, not a remembered operation: θ/°C = T/K − 273. A kelvin temperature below 273 K must give a negative Celsius temperature.

Working: θ/°C = T/K − 273 = 112 − 273 = −161, so θ = −161 °C.
items.specStatementText: that Kelvin and Celsius scales are used to express temperature

items.q: Sample P is warmed from 10 °C to 30 °C. Sample Q is warmed from 290 K to 310 K. Which statement about the two temperature changes is correct?
items.correct: Both undergo the same temperature change, 20 K.
items.misconception: P's rise of 20 °C is equivalent to a rise of 293 K.
items.why:
Students are drilled to 'always convert to kelvin' and apply the rule mechanically to ΔT in Q = mcΔT or ΔQ/Δt = −kA(ΔT/Δx), without asking whether the quantity is a temperature or a difference. Add 273 only to a temperature. A change of 60 °C is a change of 60 K; adding 273 would claim a change of 333 K, larger than the whole range from absolute zero to room temperature.

Working: P: ΔT = 30 °C − 10 °C = 20 °C = 20 K. Q: ΔT = 310 K − 290 K = 20 K. Equal changes. (P in kelvin: 283 K to 303 K, ratio 1.07, not 3.)
items.specStatementText: that the change in temperature of a system is the same when expressed with the Kelvin or Celsius scales
items.random_wrong: The changes differ, since kelvins and °C differ in size.
items.working: P: ΔT = 30 °C − 10 °C = 20 °C = 20 K. Q: ΔT = 310 K − 290 K = 20 K. Equal changes. (P in kelvin: 283 K to 303 K, ratio 1.07, not 3.)

items.q: The average kinetic energy of the molecules of a gas is 8.28 × 10⁻²¹ J. Take k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. What is the temperature of the gas in degrees Celsius?
items.why:
Students are told correctly that one kelvin equals one degree Celsius, and over-generalize from equal-sized degrees to identical scales. The old name 'degrees Kelvin' reinforces this. Same size, different zero. The Kelvin zero is absolute zero, −273 °C, so every kelvin value is 273 more than the Celsius value of the same temperature.

Working: E̅_k = (3/2)k_B T ⇒ T = 2E̅_k/(3k_B) = (2 × 8.28 × 10⁻²¹ J)/(3 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹) = 400 K. θ = 400 − 273 = 127 °C.
items.specStatementText: that Kelvin temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles as given by E̅_k = (3/2)k_B T

items.q: A sealed container of gas is heated from 20 °C to 40 °C. A student claims that the average kinetic energy of the gas molecules has doubled. Which evaluation of the claim is correct?
items.correct: Incorrect: T rises from 293 K to 313 K, so E̅_k increases by only about 7%.
items.misconception: Correct: E̅_k is proportional to temperature, and the temperature has doubled.
items.why:
Everyday temperatures are given in °C, and in Q = mcΔT (where only a difference appears) the scale does not matter, so students do not see why it matters elsewhere. Ask whether the equation contains T itself or only ΔT. If T itself appears (E̅_k = (3/2)k_B T, L = σAT⁴, λ_max T = constant, or any ratio T₂/T₁), convert to kelvin first. From 20 °C to 40 °C the absolute temperature rises only from 293 K to 313 K.

Working: T₁ = 20 + 273 = 293 K; T₂ = 40 + 273 = 313 K. E̅_k ∝ T, so E̅_k₂/E̅_k₁ = 313/293 = 1.07, an increase of about 7%, not a doubling.
items.specStatementText: that Kelvin temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles as given by E̅_k = (3/2)k_B T
items.random_wrong: Incorrect: E̅_k cannot be judged unless the amount of gas is known.
items.working: T₁ = 20 + 273 = 293 K; T₂ = 40 + 273 = 313 K. E̅_k ∝ T, so E̅_k₂/E̅_k₁ = 313/293 = 1.07, an increase of about 7%, not a doubling.

items.q: Which of the following is the internal energy of a system?
items.correct: The total random kinetic energy of its molecules plus their total intermolecular potential energy
items.misconception: The total random kinetic energy of its molecules, which is the quantity its temperature measures
items.why: Internal energy is often introduced alongside temperature and particle speed, and the potential-energy part is invisible in everyday experience, so students keep only the kinetic part. Both parts count. The potential-energy part is what changes during melting and boiling, when energy is absorbed with no change in temperature.
items.specStatementText: that the internal energy of a system is the total intermolecular potential energy arising from the forces between the molecules plus the total random kinetic energy of the molecules arising from their random motion
items.random_wrong: The kinetic energy of the body's motion plus its gravitational potential energy and its molecules' energy

items.q: A block of ice at 0 °C melts completely to give water at 0 °C. What happens to the internal energy of the H₂O, and why?
items.correct: It increases: intermolecular potential energy rises; the average kinetic energy is unchanged.
items.misconception: It is unchanged: the temperature is still 0 °C, and internal energy depends on temperature alone.
items.why: For an ideal gas (topic B.3) internal energy does depend only on temperature, and students generalize this to all substances. Everyday experience links 'energy' closely with 'hotness'. In melting ice at 0 °C the average kinetic energy stays the same, but the latent heat absorbed increases the intermolecular potential energy, so the internal energy increases while the temperature does not.
items.specStatementText: that the internal energy of a system is the total intermolecular potential energy arising from the forces between the molecules plus the total random kinetic energy of the molecules arising from their random motion
items.random_wrong: It is unchanged: the energy that is absorbed is balanced by the energy released as bonds break.

items.q: A 0.20 kg copper block at 80 °C is lowered into a large tank containing 200 kg of water at 20 °C. The water has far more internal energy than the block. Which statement describes the resultant thermal energy transfer?
items.correct: From the block to the water, until they reach the same temperature.
items.misconception: From the water to the block, since the water has more internal energy.
items.why: Everyday language uses 'heat' for both temperature and energy ('turn up the heat'), and this heat–temperature conflation is among the most persistent misconceptions reported in thermal physics (e.g. Erickson; Wiser and Carey). Keep an intensive quantity (temperature, an average per particle) apart from extensive ones (internal energy, energy transferred, which grow with the amount of substance). The direction of the resultant transfer is set by temperature alone.
items.specStatementText: that temperature difference determines the direction of the resultant thermal energy transfer between bodies
items.random_wrong: Coldness passes from the water into the block, so the block cools down.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes evaporation from boiling for water at atmospheric pressure?
items.correct: Evaporation occurs only at the surface and at any temperature; boiling occurs throughout, at the boiling point.
items.misconception: Evaporation occurs only at the boiling point, and only at the surface; boiling occurs throughout the whole liquid.
items.why: 'Evaporation' is often introduced in the same lesson as boiling and heating, and students do not observe puddles drying as a process at room temperature. Some surface molecules always have enough kinetic energy to escape, so a puddle dries at 15 °C. Boiling is different: vapour forms throughout the liquid, in bubbles, once the boiling point is reached.
items.specStatementText: that a phase change represents a change in particle behaviour arising from a change in energy at constant temperature
items.random_wrong: Boiling produces bubbles of air or of hydrogen and oxygen; evaporation produces water vapour.

items.q: A solid is heated by a heater of constant power. Its temperature rises steadily to 80 °C, stays at 80 °C for 5 minutes while the solid melts, and then rises again. Which statement about the 5 minutes at 80 °C is correct?
items.correct: Energy is absorbed and increases the intermolecular potential energy; the average kinetic energy is constant.
items.misconception: Energy is absorbed and makes the molecules move faster, although the temperature reading does not change.
items.why: In most heating that students meet, supplying energy raises the temperature, so they link energy input automatically to faster particles. Use the temperature as the guide: while it stays constant, E̅_k = (3/2)k_B T stays constant. The latent heat goes into changing the arrangement and separation of the molecules, which increases their potential energy.
items.specStatementText: that a phase change represents a change in particle behaviour arising from a change in energy at constant temperature
items.random_wrong: No energy is absorbed by the substance, because its temperature is not changing during this time.

items.q: An electric kettle heats 250 g of water from 18 °C to 90 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. How much energy is transferred to the water? Ignore energy transferred to the kettle and surroundings.
items.why:
Both are called 'temperature' in everyday speech, and many GCSE questions start at 0 °C or 20 °C, so students rarely have to keep them apart. Write ΔT = T_final − T_initial explicitly. Heating water from 18 °C to 90 °C gives ΔT = 72 K, not 90 K; a block at 20 °C that warms by 46 K ends at 66 °C.

Working: m = 250 g = 0.250 kg; ΔT = 90 − 18 = 72 K. Q = mcΔT = (0.250 kg)(4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)(72 K) = 0.250 × 4180 × 72 = 75 240 J ≈ 7.5 × 10⁴ J.
items.specStatementText: quantitative analysis of thermal energy transfers Q with the use of specific heat capacity c and specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization of substances L as given by Q = mcΔT and Q = mL

items.q: 0.40 kg of ice at 0 °C is melted and the water is then warmed to 20 °C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; specific latent heat of vaporization of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the total energy that must be supplied?
items.why:
Students equate 'energy transferred' with 'temperature change' (heat–temperature conflation), so a flat section on a heating curve looks like a pause in heating. The heater keeps supplying energy at the same rate during the plateau, and the substance absorbs it. Melting 1 kg of ice at 0 °C needs 3.34 × 10⁵ J, as much as heating that water through about 80 K.

Working: Q₁ = mL_f = (0.40 kg)(3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹) = 1.336 × 10⁵ J. Q₂ = mcΔT = (0.40 kg)(4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)(20 K) = 3.344 × 10⁴ J. Q = Q₁ + Q₂ = 1.670 × 10⁵ J ≈ 1.7 × 10⁵ J.
items.specStatementText: quantitative analysis of thermal energy transfers Q with the use of specific heat capacity c and specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization of substances L as given by Q = mcΔT and Q = mL

items.q: A 0.50 kg block of aluminium and a 0.50 kg block of copper, both at 20 °C, are each supplied with 9.0 kJ of energy. Specific heat capacities: aluminium 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, copper 390 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Assume no energy is lost. Which statement about their final temperatures is correct?
items.correct: The copper ends at about 66 °C and the aluminium at 40 °C.
items.misconception: The aluminium ends at about 66 °C, the copper at 40 °C.
items.why:
The word 'capacity' suggests an ability to absorb heat quickly, and students link 'good at taking in heat' with 'gets hot quickly'. From ΔT = Q/(mc), ΔT is inversely proportional to c. Water, with a very large c, warms slowly; copper, with a small c, warms quickly for the same energy input.

Working: ΔT = Q/(mc). Aluminium: 9000 J/(0.50 kg × 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) = 20 K, final 20 + 20 = 40 °C. Copper: 9000/(0.50 × 390) = 46.2 K, final 20 + 46 = 66 °C.
items.specStatementText: quantitative analysis of thermal energy transfers Q with the use of specific heat capacity c and specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization of substances L as given by Q = mcΔT and Q = mL
items.random_wrong: They end at the same temperature, as each gets 9.0 kJ.

items.q: Which statement about the mechanisms of thermal energy transfer is correct?
items.correct: Only thermal radiation can cross a vacuum; conduction and convection both need a medium.
items.misconception: All three are directed upwards, because heat naturally rises from warm places.
items.why: The everyday phrase 'heat rises' is a compressed version of 'hot air rises', and students treat heat as a light substance that floats. Convection moves warm fluid upwards because of density differences. The energy is carried by the fluid; the fluid is not carried by the energy. A radiant heater on a ceiling warms the floor below it.
items.specStatementText: that conduction, convection and thermal radiation are the primary mechanisms for thermal energy transfer
items.random_wrong: Convection can occur in solids as well as in liquids and gases, just like conduction.

items.q: One end of a glass rod is held in a flame. How does the molecular model explain conduction of energy along the rod?
items.correct: Faster-vibrating particles at the hot end pass kinetic energy to their slower neighbours, and so on along the rod.
items.misconception: Hot particles travel along the rod from the hot end to the cold end, carrying their energy with them.
items.why: Students merge conduction with convection, in which fluid does move, and picture energy as being carried by travelling particles. Conduction is a relay, not a journey: faster-vibrating particles at the hot end pass kinetic energy to their slower neighbours, which pass it on in turn. Only energy moves along the rod.
items.specStatementText: conduction in terms of the difference in the kinetic energy of particles
items.random_wrong: Heat flows along the rod like a fluid, filling the spaces between the particles as it goes.

items.q: A copper rod of length 0.50 m and diameter 2.0 cm is lagged along its sides. One end is kept at 100 °C and the other at 20 °C. The thermal conductivity of copper is 390 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the rate of thermal energy transfer along the rod in steady state?
items.why:
The data given in a question is often the diameter (it is what is measured with callipers), and students substitute the first length they see. Halve the diameter first, or use A = πd²/4. Because r is squared, the error is a factor of 4, not 2.

Working: r = 2.0 cm/2 = 0.010 m; A = πr² = π(0.010 m)² = 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ m². ΔT/Δx = (20 − 100) K/0.50 m = −160 K m⁻¹. ΔQ/Δt = −kA(ΔT/Δx) = −(390)(3.14 × 10⁻⁴)(−160) = +19.6 W ≈ 2.0 × 10¹ W, directed from the 100 °C end to the 20 °C end.
items.specStatementText: quantitative analysis of rate of thermal energy transfer by conduction in terms of the type of material and cross-sectional area of the material and the temperature gradient as given by ΔQ/Δt = −kA(ΔT/Δx)

items.q: The rate of thermal energy transfer by conduction is given by ΔQ/Δt = −kA(ΔT/Δx). What does the minus sign show?
items.correct: Energy flows towards lower temperature: where T falls along +x, the net flow is along +x.
items.misconception: The rate of energy transfer falls steadily with time and along the length of the conductor.
items.why: Students often read a minus sign in an equation as a label meaning 'decreases', and apply this reading to signs whose real job is to show direction (as in g = −ΔV_g/Δr). The minus sign turns a negative temperature gradient into a positive rate: where the temperature falls along +x, energy flows in the +x direction, from higher to lower temperature. In steady state the rate is constant in time and is the same through every cross-section of a uniform lagged bar.
items.specStatementText: quantitative analysis of rate of thermal energy transfer by conduction in terms of the type of material and cross-sectional area of the material and the temperature gradient as given by ΔQ/Δt = −kA(ΔT/Δx)
items.random_wrong: Cold is conducted in the opposite direction to heat, from the cold end to the hot end.

items.q: Warm air rises above a radiator in a cold room. Which is the correct explanation?
items.correct: Air heated by the radiator expands, so it is less dense than the cooler air around it, which sinks and pushes it up.
items.misconception: Each air molecule expands when it is heated, so it becomes lighter than a cold molecule and floats upwards.
items.why: Students attribute the properties of the bulk material (it expands, it becomes a gas) to the individual particles, a well-documented error in research on the particulate model (e.g. Novick and Nussbaum; Driver et al.). Macroscopic expansion is explained by particles moving further apart on average, because they move more vigorously. Particles do not swell, shrink, melt or boil; a steam molecule is identical to a water molecule.
items.specStatementText: qualitative description of thermal energy transferred by convection due to fluid density differences
items.random_wrong: Heat naturally rises, so the thermal energy from the radiator moves upwards and carries the air along with it.

items.q: A small metal sphere of radius 5.0 cm is heated to 527 °C. Treat it as a black body and take σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. What power does the sphere emit as thermal radiation?
items.why:
A star or ball looks like a flat disc, and πr² is the area formula students know best; the cross-section πr² also appears legitimately in other problems (such as the energy a planet intercepts). Use A = 4πr² for the emitting surface of a sphere and 4πd² for the sphere over which emitted power spreads. Using πr² makes the answer four times too small, or four times too large when it is in the denominator.

Working: T = 527 + 273 = 800 K. A = 4πr² = 4π(0.050 m)² = 3.14 × 10⁻² m². L = σAT⁴ = (5.67 × 10⁻⁸)(3.14 × 10⁻²)(800)⁴ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 3.14 × 10⁻² × 4.10 × 10¹¹ = 730 W ≈ 7.3 × 10² W.
items.specStatementText: quantitative analysis of energy transferred by radiation as a result of the emission of electromagnetic waves from the surface of a body, which in the case of a black body can be modelled by the Stefan-Boltzmann law as given by L = σAT⁴ where L is the luminosity, A is the surface area and T is the absolute temperature of the body

items.q: Star X has 1.2 times the radius of star Y and 1.5 times its surface temperature (in kelvin). Both stars are modelled as black bodies. What is the ratio (luminosity of X)/(luminosity of Y)?
items.why:
Students know that hotter objects glow more brightly and generalize this to stars without considering size or distance. Astronomy-education research documents it (e.g. Bailey and colleagues on students' ideas about stars). Compare both factors in L = σAT⁴: a star with 100 times the radius has 10⁴ times the area, which outweighs a temperature a few times lower. Then take distance into account through b = L/4πd².

Working: L = σAT⁴ with A = 4πr². L_X/L_Y = (r_X/r_Y)² × (T_X/T_Y)⁴ = (1.2)² × (1.5)⁴ = 1.44 × 5.0625 = 7.29 ≈ 7.3.
items.specStatementText: quantitative analysis of energy transferred by radiation as a result of the emission of electromagnetic waves from the surface of a body, which in the case of a black body can be modelled by the Stefan-Boltzmann law as given by L = σAT⁴ where L is the luminosity, A is the surface area and T is the absolute temperature of the body

items.q: Two stars appear equally bright when viewed from the Earth. Which statement must be true?
items.correct: Equal power per unit area reaches Earth from each.
items.misconception: Each star radiates the same total power out into space.
items.why: In everyday language 'bright' describes the source itself ('a bright lamp'), and students do not separate what a source emits from what arrives at the eye. The confusion is widely reported in astronomy education. Keep them separate through b = L/4πd². Two stars can look equally bright with very different luminosities if the more luminous one is further away.
items.specStatementText: the concept of apparent brightness b
items.random_wrong: The two stars are at the same distance from the Earth.

items.q: A star has a luminosity of 40 L⊙ and is 25 ly from the Earth. Take L⊙ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W and 1 ly = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. What is the apparent brightness of the star at the Earth?
items.why:
Students remember 'inverse square' as the key idea and drop the geometry that gives the area of the sphere, since 4π does not change ratios. The denominator is an area, the area of the sphere over which the power is spread: 4πd². Omitting 4π makes b about 12.6 times too large.

Working: L = 40 L⊙ = 40 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ W = 1.532 × 10²⁸ W. d = 25 × 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m = 2.365 × 10¹⁷ m. b = L/(4πd²) = 1.532 × 10²⁸/(4π × 5.593 × 10³⁴) = 1.532 × 10²⁸/7.029 × 10³⁵ = 2.2 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻².
items.specStatementText: luminosity L of a body as given by b = L/4πd²

items.q: Star P has a luminosity of 16 L⊙ and is at a distance 4d from the Earth. Star Q has a luminosity of 1 L⊙ and is at a distance d. How does the apparent brightness of P compare with that of Q?
items.correct: They appear equally bright: 16 times the luminosity offsets 4 times the distance.
items.misconception: P appears 4 times as bright as Q, as brightness is proportional to 1/d.
items.why:
Direct and inverse proportion are the first relationships students learn, and the geometric reason for the square (the area of a sphere) is not visualized. b = L/4πd²: the power spreads over the surface of a sphere of radius d, whose area grows as d². Doubling d quarters b; multiplying d by 4 divides b by 16.

Working: b = L/4πd². b_P/b_Q = (16 L⊙/(4π(4d)²))/(1 L⊙/(4πd²)) = 16/16 = 1, so the two stars appear equally bright.
items.specStatementText: luminosity L of a body as given by b = L/4πd²
items.random_wrong: P appears 16 times as bright as Q, because it is 16 times as luminous.
items.working: b = L/4πd². b_P/b_Q = (16 L⊙/(4π(4d)²))/(1 L⊙/(4πd²)) = 16/16 = 1, so the two stars appear equally bright.

items.q: A surface at 27 °C can be modelled as a black body. Wien's displacement law: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K. At what wavelength is its emission most intense?
items.correct: 9.7 × 10⁻⁶ m, in the infrared
items.misconception: 8.7 × 10⁻¹ m, in the radio band
items.why:
Everyday colour coding marks hot taps and warnings in red and cold in blue, and 'red-hot' is used for very hot things, so students link red with the hottest objects. Wien's law: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K, so λ_max ∝ 1/T. An object heated in a furnace glows dull red, then orange, then white as it gets hotter; blue-white stars are the hottest.

Working: T = 27 + 273 = 300 K. λ_max = (2.9 × 10⁻³ m K)/(300 K) = 9.7 × 10⁻⁶ m, which is in the infrared (about 10 μm).
items.specStatementText: the emission spectrum of a black body and the determination of the temperature of the body using Wien’s displacement law as given by λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K where λ_max is the peak wavelength emitted.
items.random_wrong: 1.1 × 10⁻⁴ m, in the far infrared
items.working: T = 27 + 273 = 300 K. λ_max = (2.9 × 10⁻³ m K)/(300 K) = 9.7 × 10⁻⁶ m, which is in the infrared (about 10 μm).

items.q: The black-body spectrum of star X peaks at 290 nm and that of star Y peaks at 870 nm. The two stars have the same radius. Which conclusion is correct?
items.correct: X has three times the surface temperature of Y, and 81 times its luminosity.
items.misconception: X has three times the surface temperature of Y and three times the luminosity.
items.why:
Students default to direct proportion whenever two quantities increase together, and the fourth power is easy to forget when reasoning in words. Always use the power law: L₂/L₁ = (A₂/A₁)(T₂/T₁)⁴. The strong T⁴ dependence is why a small temperature difference between stars makes a large difference in luminosity.

Working: Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K, so T_X/T_Y = λ_Y/λ_X = 870/290 = 3.0 (T_X ≈ 1.0 × 10⁴ K, T_Y ≈ 3.3 × 10³ K). Equal radii: L_X/L_Y = (T_X/T_Y)⁴ = 3⁴ = 81.
items.specStatementText: the emission spectrum of a black body and the determination of the temperature of the body using Wien’s displacement law as given by λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K where λ_max is the peak wavelength emitted.
items.random_wrong: Y has three times the surface temperature of X and has 81 times the luminosity.
items.working: Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K, so T_X/T_Y = λ_Y/λ_X = 870/290 = 3.0 (T_X ≈ 1.0 × 10⁴ K, T_Y ≈ 3.3 × 10³ K). Equal radii: L_X/L_Y = (T_X/T_Y)⁴ = 3⁴ = 81.

items.q: A black body is heated to a higher temperature. How does its emission spectrum change?
items.correct: It emits more at every wavelength, and its peak moves to a shorter wavelength.
items.misconception: Its peak moves to shorter wavelengths, so it emits less at long wavelengths.
items.why: The word 'displacement' in Wien's displacement law and sketches of curves that appear to move sideways suggest the spectrum slides along the wavelength axis rather than rising. Compare the curves at any fixed wavelength: the hotter curve is always higher. The total power, the area under the curve, grows as T⁴.
items.specStatementText: the emission spectrum of a black body and the determination of the temperature of the body using Wien’s displacement law as given by λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K where λ_max is the peak wavelength emitted.
items.random_wrong: It emits more at every wavelength, and the peak moves to a longer wavelength.

items.q: Water in an electric kettle is boiling at 100 °C. The 2.0 kW heater stays switched on for a further 2.5 minutes. Assume all the energy supplied is transferred to the water. Specific latent heat of vaporization of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. What mass of water boils away?
items.why:
'Fusion' is unfamiliar in its meaning of melting and is met elsewhere meaning 'joining' (nuclear fusion), so students cannot tell which latent heat belongs to which change and pick one at random. Match the latent heat to the change: melting ice uses L_f; boiling water uses L_v. Using L_v for a melting problem overestimates the energy by a factor of nearly seven.

Working: Q = Pt = (2.0 × 10³ W)(2.5 × 60 s) = 3.0 × 10⁵ J. The water stays at 100 °C, so all of this is latent heat of vaporization: Q = mL_v, m = Q/L_v = (3.0 × 10⁵ J)/(2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹) = 0.133 kg ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻¹ kg.
items.specStatementText: quantitative analysis of thermal energy transfers Q with the use of specific heat capacity c and specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization of substances L as given by Q = mcΔT and Q = mL
items.working: Q = Pt = (2.0 × 10³ W)(2.5 × 60 s) = 3.0 × 10⁵ J. The water stays at 100 °C, so all of this is latent heat of vaporization: Q = mL_v, m = Q/L_v = (3.0 × 10⁵ J)/(2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹) = 0.133 kg ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻¹ kg.

items.q: Two solid cubes are cut from the same block of steel. Cube X has sides of length 2.0 cm and cube Y has sides of length 4.0 cm. Which statement correctly compares cube Y with cube X?
items.correct: Y has eight times the mass of X and the same density as X.
items.misconception: Y has four times the mass of X and the same density as X.
items.why:
Students meet 'double the side, four times the area' first and carry the squared rule over to volume; the distinction between area and volume scaling is a documented difficulty in proportional reasoning (Arons). Write the volume out as a product of three lengths: (2a)(2a)(2a) = 8a³. Check with a 1 cm cube: eight of them fill a 2 cm cube.

Working: Same material ⇒ same density ρ = m/V. Volume scales as length³: V_Y/V_X = (4.0/2.0)³ = 8, so m_Y = ρV_Y = 8 m_X. Density unchanged.
items.specStatementText: density ρ as given by ρ = m/V
items.random_wrong: Y has twice the mass of X and the same density as X.
items.working: Same material ⇒ same density ρ = m/V. Volume scales as length³: V_Y/V_X = (4.0/2.0)³ = 8, so m_Y = ρV_Y = 8 m_X. Density unchanged.

items.q: Which statement about the Kelvin and Celsius temperature scales is correct?
items.correct: A Celsius temperature is converted to kelvin by adding 273, whether the Celsius value is above or below zero.
items.misconception: A temperature below the freezing point of water is negative on the Kelvin scale, exactly as it is on the Celsius scale.
items.why:
Students' experience of temperature is the Celsius scale, on which winter temperatures are negative; they treat the Kelvin scale as a relabelled Celsius scale and do not see 0 K as a physical limit. T/K = t/°C + 273 always adds 273, so any temperature above −273 °C is positive in kelvin. 0 K is where the average kinetic energy of the particles would reach its minimum; there is nothing below it.

Working: T/K = t/°C + 273 for every temperature, e.g. −78 °C → −78 + 273 = 195 K and 27 °C → 300 K; the reverse conversion subtracts 273 (112 K → −161 °C).
items.specStatementText: that Kelvin and Celsius scales are used to express temperature
items.random_wrong: A Kelvin temperature is converted to degrees Celsius by adding 273, since both directions use the same rule.
items.working: T/K = t/°C + 273 for every temperature, e.g. −78 °C → −78 + 273 = 195 K and 27 °C → 300 K; the reverse conversion subtracts 273 (112 K → −161 °C).

items.q: The specific heat capacity of copper is 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. A student heats a copper block from 15 °C to 65 °C and, before using Q = mcΔT, adds 273 to the temperature change 'because c is given per kelvin'. Which evaluation of the student's method is correct?
items.correct: It is wrong: a temperature change has the same numerical value in kelvin as in degrees Celsius, since the two scales differ only in where their zero lies.
items.misconception: It is wrong only in the number used: the kelvin and the degree Celsius are different sizes, so ΔT should be multiplied by a factor rather than have 273 added.
items.why: Students meet the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales, whose degrees are different sizes (a change of 1 °C is 1.8 °F), and the kelvin has a different name and symbol, so they assume it is another differently sized unit. The Kelvin and Celsius scales differ only in where zero is. Shifting the zero by 273 does not change the size of the step, so ΔT/K = Δθ/°C.
items.specStatementText: that the change in temperature of a system is the same when expressed with the Kelvin or Celsius scales
items.random_wrong: It is correct: every Celsius quantity, including a temperature change, must have 273 added to it before it is used in a physics equation.

items.q: A metal sphere at 33 °C hangs from a thin thread inside a large evacuated chamber whose walls are at 18 °C. Energy is exchanged between the sphere and the walls only by thermal radiation. Which statement describes the resultant thermal energy transfer?
items.correct: Both emit thermal radiation, but the sphere emits more than it absorbs, so the resultant transfer is from the sphere to the walls.
items.misconception: Only the sphere emits thermal radiation, since the walls are too cool to radiate, so the whole transfer is from the sphere to the walls.
items.why: The radiation we notice is from glowing or very hot sources, and 'radiation' in everyday language suggests something dangerous or special. L = σAT⁴ is non-zero for every T above 0 K. A person at about 305 K radiates hundreds of watts in the infrared, which is how thermal cameras work.
items.specStatementText: that temperature difference determines the direction of the resultant thermal energy transfer between bodies
items.random_wrong: The walls contain far more internal energy than the sphere does, so the resultant transfer of energy is from the walls to the sphere.

items.q: On a still evening a person stands 2 m to one side of a bonfire, at the same height as the flames, and feels warmth on their face. By which mechanism does most of this energy reach their face, and why?
items.correct: Radiation: still air is a poor conductor, and the hot air from the fire rises, so neither conduction nor convection carries much energy sideways.
items.misconception: Conduction: the hot air next to the flames passes energy from particle to particle across the 2 m of still air to the person's face.
items.why: Everyday speech says 'the heat comes through the air' and students know conduction as 'heat passing through a material'; air is not recognized as an insulator because it is invisible and not a solid. Trapped air is the working part of most insulation (double glazing, fleece, loft insulation). Hold a card between your face and a fire: the warmth stops at once, which conduction or convection through the air could not explain.
items.specStatementText: that conduction, convection and thermal radiation are the primary mechanisms for thermal energy transfer
items.random_wrong: Convection: heat is a fluid that spreads out from the fire through the air in every direction, including sideways to the face.

items.q: One end of a steel rod is held at 80 °C and the other at 20 °C. After some time the temperature at every point along the rod stops changing. Which statement about the particles of the rod is correct in this steady state?
items.correct: Particles near the hot end still have more kinetic energy on average than those near the cold end, and kinetic energy is still being passed along the rod towards the cold end.
items.misconception: Every particle along the rod now vibrates with the same kinetic energy; what decreases towards the cold end is the amount of heat stored between the particles.
items.why: Everyday language ('keep the heat in', 'heat flows') and the historical caloric theory both treat heat as a substance; this is one of the most thoroughly documented misconceptions in thermal physics (e.g. Erickson; Harrison, Grayson and Treagust). Talk about internal energy for what a body has and thermal energy transfer for what passes between bodies because of a temperature difference. Nothing material flows: energy is passed on through particle interactions or electromagnetic radiation.
items.specStatementText: conduction in terms of the difference in the kinetic energy of particles
items.random_wrong: Since the temperature at every point along the rod has stopped changing, no more energy is now being transferred from the hot end to the cold end.

items.q: In a simple refrigerator the freezing compartment is placed at the top of the cabinet. Which statement explains why this cools the whole of the space below it?
items.correct: Air cooled by the compartment becomes denser and sinks, and the warmer air below rises to replace it, so a convection current circulates.
items.misconception: Coldness is a heavy substance that is produced by the compartment and pours down through the cabinet, filling it from the bottom upwards like water.
items.why: Everyday speech ('shut the door, you'll let the cold in', 'the cold seeps in') treats cold as something that moves; the misconception is widely documented in research on students' ideas about heat (e.g. Erickson; Lewis and Linn). Describe every case as energy moving from hot to cold. A metal rail 'feels cold' because energy is conducted rapidly out of the hand into it; nothing flows from the rail into the hand.
items.specStatementText: qualitative description of thermal energy transferred by convection due to fluid density differences
items.random_wrong: Heat naturally rises, so the thermal energy from all the food travels upwards to the compartment at the top, where it is removed from the cabinet.

items.q: Star A has 100 times the luminosity of star B, yet from the Earth star A appears dimmer than star B. Which statement must be correct?
items.correct: A lies much further from the Earth than B does.
items.misconception: At equal distances, A and B would look equally bright.
items.why: Everyday experience with identical lamps (street lights) shows nearer ones look brighter, and students assume stars are all alike. Stars differ in luminosity by factors of millions. A nearby dim star can look fainter than a distant luminous one; both L and d must be known to compare brightnesses.
items.specStatementText: the concept of apparent brightness b
items.random_wrong: We receive more power per unit area from A than from B.

items.q: Are the particles in a solid moving?
items.correct: Yes. They vibrate continuously about fixed mean positions; the vibration becomes more vigorous as the temperature rises.
items.misconception: The particles of a solid are completely still; they start to move only when the solid melts.
items.why: Textbook diagrams show solid particles as a neat, motionless grid, and a solid visibly does not flow. Students transfer the stillness of the object to its particles. All particles above absolute zero have random kinetic energy. In a solid, strong intermolecular forces hold them in fixed mean positions, so their random motion is vibration about those positions. Melting lets them move past one another; it does not start their motion.
items.specStatementText: molecular theory in solids, liquids and gases
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do gases, including hot air and steam, have mass?
items.correct: Yes. The molecules of a gas have exactly the same mass as in the liquid or solid; a gas has a low density because its molecules are far apart, not because they are lighter.
items.misconception: Gases (and hot air in particular) have little or no mass or weight, so gas molecules must be lighter than liquid molecules.
items.why: Air cannot be felt or seen and things 'float' in it; hot air balloons and rising smoke suggest that hot gas is weightless. The belief that gases weigh nothing is documented in children's and students' ideas about matter (e.g. Stavy; Séré). Mass is conserved when water boils: 1 kg of water makes 1 kg of steam. Hot air rises only because a given volume of it has less mass than the same volume of cooler air around it, so the denser surrounding air pushes it up.
items.specStatementText: molecular theory in solids, liquids and gases
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is density mass divided by volume, or volume divided by mass?
items.correct: Density is mass divided by volume, ρ = m/V, in kg m⁻³. Volume divided by mass is a different quantity (volume per kilogram, in m³ kg⁻¹).
items.misconception: Density can be found by dividing the volume by the mass.
items.why: Students remember that density 'involves mass and volume' but not which is on top, and recall the formula as a word pair rather than as a definition. Density is 'mass per unit volume', so mass is divided by volume. Checking the unit (kg m⁻³) or the size of the answer (metals are thousands of kg m⁻³) catches the inversion.
items.specStatementText: density ρ as given by ρ = m/V
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When converting a temperature below 273 K to Celsius, can the subtraction be done either way round?
items.correct: No. θ = T − 273, so a temperature below 273 K gives a negative Celsius temperature: 112 K = 112 − 273 = −161 °C.
items.misconception: To convert kelvin to Celsius, subtract the smaller number from the larger, so the result is always positive.
items.why: Students avoid negative numbers by always subtracting the smaller from the larger, and do not check that a temperature below the melting point of ice must be below 0 °C. Write θ = T − 273 and substitute. Check the sign: any temperature below 273 K is colder than melting ice and must be negative in °C.
items.specStatementText: that Kelvin and Celsius scales are used to express temperature
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the average kinetic energy of a particle equal to k_B T?
items.correct: No. E̅_k = (3/2)k_B T. The factor 3/2 arises because the translational motion has three independent directions, each contributing ½k_B T on average.
items.misconception: The average kinetic energy of a particle is simply k_B T, 'the thermal energy'.
items.why: Chemistry and some physics texts describe k_B T loosely as 'the thermal energy' of a particle when making order-of-magnitude comparisons, and students carry the phrase into calculations and drop the numerical factor. Use the full relationship E̅_k = (3/2)k_B T, so T = 2E̅_k/(3k_B). Treating k_B T as E̅_k makes the calculated temperature 1.5 times too large.
items.specStatementText: that Kelvin temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles as given by E̅_k = (3/2)k_B T
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a body's internal energy increase if the body is moving faster or is raised higher?
items.correct: No. Internal energy concerns only the random motion of molecules and the forces between them. The kinetic energy of the body as a whole and its gravitational potential energy are separate, macroscopic stores.
items.misconception: Internal energy is all the energy a body has, including the kinetic energy of its motion as a whole and its gravitational potential energy.
items.why: The word 'internal' is read loosely as 'all the energy the object has', and A.3 mechanics has just taught students to add every energy store together. Internal energy is energy on the molecular scale: random kinetic energy and intermolecular potential energy. A thermos flask carried up a hill gains gravitational potential energy but its internal energy is unchanged.
items.specStatementText: that the internal energy of a system is the total intermolecular potential energy arising from the forces between the molecules plus the total random kinetic energy of the molecules arising from their random motion
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is energy released when the bonds or attractions between molecules are broken?
items.correct: No. Separating molecules against their mutual attraction requires energy, so breaking intermolecular bonds absorbs energy and raises the potential energy. Energy is released when bonds form (freezing, condensing).
items.misconception: Breaking the bonds between molecules releases energy, so melting or boiling lowers the potential energy.
items.why: Students learn that fuels and food 'release energy from their bonds' and conclude that breaking any bond releases energy. This is a well-documented misconception in chemistry education (e.g. Boo; Barker and Millar). Energy is needed to pull attracting particles apart, just as energy is needed to lift a mass away from the Earth. Melting and boiling absorb latent heat and increase intermolecular potential energy; freezing and condensing release it.
items.specStatementText: that the internal energy of a system is the total intermolecular potential energy arising from the forces between the molecules plus the total random kinetic energy of the molecules arising from their random motion
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When two bodies in contact reach thermal equilibrium, do they have equal internal energies?
items.correct: No. They have equal temperatures. Their internal energies can be very different, depending on their masses, materials and phases.
items.misconception: Energy flows between two bodies until they contain the same amount of internal energy (or 'heat').
items.why: Students picture energy as a fluid that levels out like water between connected tanks, and conflate the level (temperature) with the quantity (internal energy). The resultant transfer stops when the temperatures are equal. A small hot metal block dropped into a large tank of water ends up at almost the water's temperature, with much less internal energy than the water.
items.specStatementText: that temperature difference determines the direction of the resultant thermal energy transfer between bodies
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are the bubbles that form in boiling water made of?
items.correct: Water vapour (steam): water molecules that have changed from liquid to gas inside the liquid.
items.misconception: The bubbles in boiling water are air, or hydrogen and oxygen produced as water breaks down.
items.why: Small bubbles of dissolved air do appear as water warms, and students know water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. Osborne and Cosgrove documented both beliefs in their study of students' ideas about boiling. Boiling is a phase change, not a chemical change: the bubbles are water in the gas phase. When the heating stops they collapse because the vapour condenses back to liquid.
items.specStatementText: that a phase change represents a change in particle behaviour arising from a change in energy at constant temperature
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If a liquid keeps being heated while it boils, does its temperature keep rising?
items.correct: No. At constant pressure a pure liquid stays at its boiling point while it boils; extra heating makes it boil faster, not hotter.
items.misconception: The temperature of a boiling liquid keeps rising as long as it is heated, so the energy supplied to it goes into raising its temperature.
items.why: Students associate heating with rising temperature and expect a hotter flame to give hotter boiling water. The energy supplied during boiling is used as latent heat of vaporization at constant temperature. Turning up the heater increases the rate of boiling, not the temperature.
items.specStatementText: that a phase change represents a change in particle behaviour arising from a change in energy at constant temperature
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can convection transfer energy through a solid?
items.correct: No. Convection needs bulk movement of the material, which can happen only in fluids (liquids and gases). Energy passes through solids by conduction.
items.misconception: Convection can take place in solids, for example when a metal rod heated at one end gets hot at the other end.
items.why: Students learn the three mechanisms as three names and attach 'convection' to anything that 'carries heat', without the idea that the material itself must move. Ask whether the material itself moves from place to place. In a solid the particles only vibrate about fixed positions, so energy moves through it by conduction, not convection.
items.specStatementText: that conduction, convection and thermal radiation are the primary mechanisms for thermal energy transfer
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the minus sign in the conduction equation mean that the material loses energy, so ΔQ/Δt is always negative?
items.correct: No. In steady-state conduction the material gains as much energy at the hot face as it loses at the cold face; the minus sign expresses the direction of flow relative to the temperature gradient, and ΔQ/Δt is positive in the direction of decreasing temperature.
items.misconception: The minus sign means the conductor is losing energy, so the rate of transfer through any material is always a negative quantity.
items.why: Students meet 'energy lost' in many contexts and associate negative values with losses, so a minus sign in a transfer equation is read as a loss. Read the sign with the gradient: temperature falling along +x gives a negative ΔT/Δx and a positive ΔQ/Δt along +x. The sign of the result tells you which way the energy goes, not that energy is lost.
items.specStatementText: quantitative analysis of rate of thermal energy transfer by conduction in terms of the type of material and cross-sectional area of the material and the temperature gradient as given by ΔQ/Δt = −kA(ΔT/Δx)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does Wien's displacement law involve T⁴?
items.correct: No. Wien's law is λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K, with T to the first power. The fourth power belongs to the Stefan–Boltzmann law, L = σAT⁴.
items.misconception: Wien's law and the Stefan–Boltzmann law can be mixed: the peak wavelength depends on T⁴.
items.why: Both laws describe black-body radiation, are taught in the same lesson and both involve the absolute temperature, so students blend their forms. Keep the two laws apart by what they give: Stefan–Boltzmann gives the total power (T⁴); Wien gives the position of the peak (1/T).
items.specStatementText: the emission spectrum of a black body and the determination of the temperature of the body using Wien’s displacement law as given by λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K where λ_max is the peak wavelength emitted.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the colour (peak wavelength) of a star determined by what it is made of?
items.correct: No. A star's continuous spectrum is approximately a black-body spectrum, and its peak wavelength, and hence its colour, is set by its surface temperature through Wien's law.
items.misconception: The colour of a star, and the wavelength at which it emits most strongly, depends on the chemical elements in it rather than on its temperature.
items.why: Students learn that flame tests and spectral lines identify elements by colour, and transfer this to the overall colour of a star. Absorption lines in a star's spectrum reveal its composition, but the overall shape of the continuous spectrum, including the peak, depends on temperature. A star peaking at a shorter wavelength is hotter, whatever it is made of.
items.specStatementText: the emission spectrum of a black body and the determination of the temperature of the body using Wien’s displacement law as given by λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K where λ_max is the peak wavelength emitted.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a black body emit only its peak wavelength?
items.correct: No. A black body emits a continuous spectrum over all wavelengths; λ_max is only the wavelength at which the intensity is greatest.
items.misconception: A black body emits radiation at just one wavelength, λ_max, which changes as its temperature changes.
items.why: Wien's law is written in terms of a single wavelength, and the colour name of a star ('red', 'blue') suggests a single colour of light. The black-body curve spreads over a wide range of wavelengths. A star that looks white emits all visible wavelengths; λ_max only tells you where the curve peaks.
items.specStatementText: the emission spectrum of a black body and the determination of the temperature of the body using Wien’s displacement law as given by λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K where λ_max is the peak wavelength emitted.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a larger or heavier piece of a material denser than a smaller piece of the same material?
items.correct: No. Density is a property of the material, not of the amount of it: mass and volume grow in the same proportion, so ρ = m/V is unchanged. Two steel cubes of different sizes have the same density.
items.misconception: Density is a measure of how much material or how heavy an object is, so a bigger or heavier object made of the same substance is denser.
items.why: Everyday use of 'dense' and 'heavy' overlaps, and children's first idea of density is undifferentiated from weight; the failure to separate density (intensive) from mass (extensive) is one of the best-documented findings in research on students' ideas about matter (e.g. Smith, Carey and Wiser on the differentiation of weight and density). Cut a block in half: each half has half the mass and half the volume, so the same density. Density identifies the material; mass tells you how much of it there is.
items.specStatementText: density ρ as given by ρ = m/V
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
